opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we wrestle with constantly, and I think the honest answer is that you have to treat it as a portfolio decision rather than a one-time bet.

The first thing I look at is what problem the fine-tuning is actually solving. If you're fine-tuning to make up for a general capability gap, like the model isn't quite good enough at reasoning or following complex instructions, that's exactly the kind of investment that tends to get washed away by the next generation. The base models keep getting better at those things, and you can find yourself having spent months on something a new release does out of the box.

But if the fine-tuning encodes something that's genuinely specific to you, like your domain's terminology, your organization's policies, a particular tone or format your users expect, or safety behaviors tailored to your context, that knowledge doesn't come for free with a bigger model. The next model won't magically know your internal workflows. That kind of work tends to hold its value much better.

The second thing is to protect the parts that carry over. In practice, the most durable assets usually aren't the fine-tuned weights themselves. They're the data you curated, the evaluation sets you built, and the understanding of what "good" looks like for your application. If you've invested in really strong evaluations, then when a new model comes out you can quickly measure whether it beats your fine-tuned version, whether you should re-tune on top of it, or whether prompting and retrieval now get you there. So I often tell teams: even if you never ship a fine-tuned model, building the evaluation and data pipeline is almost never wasted.

Third, be realistic about the time horizon. If the payoff is in production next month and saves real cost or latency, maybe by distilling into a smaller model, the math can work even if it's obsolete in a year. If it's a long research project chasing frontier capability, you're racing the model providers, and that's usually a race you don't want to be in.

And finally, I always encourage people to start with the cheaper levers first: prompt engineering, retrieval, good system design. A lot of the time that gets you most of the way, and then fine-tuning becomes a targeted tool for the last mile rather than the foundation of your whole approach. That way, when the next generation lands, you're positioned to take advantage of it instead of being stuck defending a sunk cost.

r001.rationale: The response says a payoff in production next month can make fine-tuning worthwhile even if it becomes obsolete in a year. That communicates the value of getting near-term production benefits before a later model arrives.

r002.rationale: It warns against long projects chasing frontier capability, but does not advise against investing merely because an outperforming later model would make the investor regard the work as wasted.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I think about a lot, because it's the question every customer asks us, and honestly it's one we ask ourselves internally at Microsoft. My short answer is that fine-tuning is worth it when the thing you're teaching the model is something the next generation can't learn on its own.

Let me unpack that. There are really two different reasons people fine-tune. The first is to make up for a capability gap. The base model isn't quite good enough at reasoning over your domain, or it doesn't follow a complex format reliably, so you fine-tune to push it over the line. That kind of fine-tuning is exactly the kind that gets obsoleted. We've seen it over and over: someone spends three months fine-tuning for a capability, and then the next model release does it zero-shot out of the box. If that's your motivation, I'd be pretty cautious. You should at least ask whether a better prompt, retrieval, or just waiting six months gets you there cheaper.

The second reason is to encode knowledge or behavior that is specific to you. Your proprietary data, your tone of voice, your particular safety policy, your domain terminology that just doesn't exist on the public internet. No frontier model release is going to know your internal product catalog or how your support team is supposed to talk to customers. That investment doesn't go stale in the same way. The weights you trained might, but the data you curated and the evaluation you built to prove it worked carry straight over to the next model.

And that's really the part I'd emphasize. The durable asset is almost never the fine-tuned checkpoint. It's the data pipeline and the eval. If you've done the work to build a high-quality dataset that represents your task, and a rigorous evaluation that tells you whether a model is actually good at it, then when the new generation ships you just rerun the recipe. Maybe you find you don't need to fine-tune anymore, which is a great outcome. Maybe you still do, and it takes you a week instead of three months.

There's also an economics angle. A lot of fine-tuning today isn't about capability at all, it's about getting a small model to do what a big model does, so you can serve it at a fraction of the cost and latency. That tradeoff keeps being valuable even as the frontier moves, because the frontier always costs more than you'd like at scale.

So the way I'd frame the decision is: don't fine-tune to chase the frontier, fine-tune to encode what's uniquely yours, and put your real investment in the data and the evaluation rather than the model artifact. If you do that, the next generation isn't a threat to your work, it's a free upgrade.

r001.rationale: The response does not say that getting an application to market sooner can justify fine-tuning before a later model release.

r002.rationale: It advises caution for fine-tuning to close capability gaps and suggests considering alternatives or waiting, but does not advise against investing on the stated condition that a later model would make the investor regard the investment as wasted.

astra-6.text:
I think you have to start with the problem you’re trying to solve and the time horizon. If fine-tuning gets you a meaningful improvement in quality or cost for something you need to deploy today, it can be worth doing even if a future model eventually gives you that capability out of the box. The investment doesn’t have to last forever to pay off.

But I would establish a baseline first. How far can you get with prompting, or with retrieval if the issue is access to information? Then ask whether fine-tuning closes a specific gap, and whether that improvement justifies the work of maintaining it.

The part I’d really invest in is the evaluation: understanding what good looks like for your application, collecting representative examples, and being able to measure whether a change helps. That’s useful whether you fine-tune the current model or move to the next generation. When a new model arrives, you can run the same evaluation and make that decision based on evidence.

r001.rationale: It says fine-tuning can be worth doing to improve quality or cost for a deployment needed today, even if a future model later provides that capability.

r002.rationale: It does not advise against fine-tuning when the investor would view it as wasted if a later model outperforms it; it instead says the investment need not last forever to pay off.

sol-6.1.text:
I think you have to start with what you need the model to do and where it’s falling short today. Is it missing information? Is it struggling to follow your instructions consistently? Or do you need a particular behavior that you can’t reliably get through prompting? Those are different problems, and fine-tuning isn’t necessarily the right answer to all of them.

I’d invest in an evaluation set first. If you can measure the gap, you can try prompting, retrieval, and fine-tuning and see what actually helps. Then the question becomes: does the improvement create enough value over the period you expect to use this model to justify the cost?

And some of that investment carries forward. The examples you collect, the understanding of your task, and the evaluations you build will help you assess the next model, too. You may not need the same fine-tuning next time, but you’ll have a much better way to decide.

r001.rationale: The response weighs improvement against cost over the model’s expected use period, but does not say that bringing an application to market sooner can justify fine-tuning.

r002.rationale: The response does not advise against investing when a later model might make the fine-tuning obsolete or lead the investor to view it as wasted.
